ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Elizabeth Barrett Browning Synthetic CCD — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: New patient visit for chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, a long-term opioid prescription, and grief, with tuberculosis testing and urgent pulmonology referral. Concerns: She has coughed for years and lately sees streaks of blood; she wants to know whether it is consumption; She worries that the morphine she has taken for so long is harming her, but fears being made to stop it; She wants to keep writing, and to be able to think of her brother without being overwhelmed. [S]

tr.td: Serious illness at about fifteen, from which she nearly died, treated at a spa for most of a year; a spinal injury, later attributed to a strain, contributed to lasting weakness; a prescribed opiate from then on
Chest illness with blood in the sputum (described as a broken blood vessel), judged by her physicians to be an affection of the lungs but not tubercular consumption; largely confined indoors since
Severe decline in health after the drowning of her brother, with slow recovery over the following winter

list.item: Chronic cough with daily yellow sputum, occasional streaks of blood, and breathlessness on stairs, worse in winter, for several years after an illness with blood in the sputum about eight years ago; tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria and bronchiectasis to be distinguished: resolved, confirmed [S]

Non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis of the left lower lobe and lingula with chronic Haemophilus influenzae infection and mild airflow obstruction (Bronchiectasis Severity Index 3, mild); tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease excluded; synthetic modern diagnosis chosen for a historical chest illness whose cause is disputed: active, confirmed [S]

Long-term prescribed opioid therapy (oral morphine 20 mg a day for many years, for cough, sleeplessness and palpitations), with expected physiological dependence; no opioid use disorder on DSM-5-TR assessment: active, confirmed [S]

Prolonged grief disorder after the drowning of her closest brother five years ago, with yearning, self-blame, avoidance of reminders of the sea, and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 12); no suicidal ideation: active, confirmed [S]
Vitamin D deficiency (25-hydroxyvitamin D 15 ng/mL) in a woman who rarely goes outdoors: resolved, confirmed [S]
Underweight (BMI 16.8) with a small appetite: active, confirmed [S]

Exacerbation of bronchiectasis (more sputum, purulent sputum, more cough and breathlessness for three days, with low-grade fever), treated with amoxicillin for 14 days and more frequent airway clearance; resolved: resolved, confirmed [S]

tr.td: New patient visit for chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, a long-term opioid prescription, and grief, with tuberculosis testing and urgent pulmonology referral
Pulmonology consultation with CT of the chest and spirometry, diagnosis of bronchiectasis, and the start of airway clearance
Four-week review: mycobacterial cultures, airway clearance, bone density, grief therapy, and her choice about the opioid dose
Three-month review: final mycobacterial cultures, vitamin D, mood, safety, and the opioid dose
Seven-month review after an exacerbation: lungs, opioid therapy, mood, safety, weight, and vaccines
Same-day sick visit for an exacerbation of bronchiectasis

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Evaluation of chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum: three sputum samples at least eight hours apart, one early morning, for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture (including nontuberculous mycobacteria) and routine bacterial culture; interferon-gamma release assay and HIV test; blood count, CRP and metabolic panel; CT of the chest within a week; a mask in shared spaces until the smears are negative; call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, or chest pain

Urgent pulmonology consultation within one week for chronic productive cough with blood-streaked sputum: exclude tuberculosis, confirm or exclude bronchiectasis and plan its care, and advise on opioids and the lungs

Long-term opioid therapy review: prescription monitoring program checked (one prescriber, one pharmacy), urine drug test consistent with morphine only, naloxone prescribed and taught, no benzodiazepines or other sedatives, DSM-5-TR assessment (no opioid use disorder), dose continued unchanged with no forced taper, benefits and harms reviewed at every visit and at least every three months, the monitoring program checked with every prescription, and buprenorphine offered if opioid use disorder ever develops
Prolonged grief disorder therapy with the clinic psychologist, weekly for sixteen sessions, by video at first so she need not travel; PHQ-9 at every visit

Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; morphine kept in a locked box with only the current bottle out; safety reviewed at every visit

Bone and nutrition: vitamin D3 1819 units daily with a recheck at twelve weeks; DXA for low weight, vitamin D deficiency, limited weight-bearing and long-term opioid therapy; calcium-rich foods, small frequent meals and an oral supplement drink with the clinic dietitian; weight at every visit

Bronchiectasis care: active cycle of breathing with an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device twice daily, taught by the respiratory physiotherapist; a home exercise program; influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccines; a written exacerbation plan with a sputum sample and amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days; sputum culture at each review and spirometry, Bronchiectasis Severity Index and mycobacterial culture yearly; no long-term macrolide while exacerbations are fewer than three a year

Opioid dose reduction at her request: morphine lowered by about 10 percent at a time (to 18 mg a day now), with each step held at least four weeks, paused at any time she wishes, and never forced; withdrawal symptoms and sleep reviewed at each visit

Exacerbation of bronchiectasis: sputum culture before the first dose; amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days; airway clearance three to four times a day; fluids; the morphine dose unchanged and no added cough suppressant; nurse phone check in two days; call 911 for more than a few teaspoons of blood, worsening breathlessness or confusion
Tuberculosis excluded and a diagnosis for the cough within two weeks
Smears, NAAT and IGRA negative within a week; bronchiectasis diagnosed by CT at one week
Airway clearance twice daily, with less sputum and no blood in it, by three months
Airway clearance twice daily; sputum down from about four to one tablespoon a day; no blood since the first month
Safe opioid therapy: naloxone at home, no overdose or sedation, and any dose change only by her choice
Naloxone at home; no sedation; she chose to reduce from 20 to 14 mg a day over seven months without troublesome withdrawal
Response of grief and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 down by at least half) by six months
PHQ-9 5 from 12 after sixteen sessions of grief therapy; she can speak of her brother
Weight up toward a BMI of 18.5 (45.6 kg) by seven months
Vitamin D above 30 ng/mL by twelve weeks

list.item: Independent in personal care; breathless after one flight of stairs; spends most of the day on a sofa; writes for several hours a day [S]
Alert, articulate and warm; mood 'heavy'; tearful when her brother is mentioned; thought content without suicidal ideation, intent or plan; PHQ-9 score 12 [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 1845-03-16: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with a collaborative safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, her morphine kept in a locked box with only the current bottle out, naloxone at home, and review at every visit [S]
